newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo seen heading for centralised banking system.
newsitem.headline: Yugo seen heading for centralised banking system.

text.p: Yugoslavia's troubled banks will soon embark on a rehabilitation programme which analysts saw as leading to a centralised banking system giving the government more control over scarce financial resources.
But economists said any centralisation of the banking system was in conflict with the government's proclaimed commitment to developing a liberal and open market economy.

Some bankers, however, welcomed an independent bank overhaul initiative coming from the largest Yugoslav banking group Beogradska Banka, headed by Borka Vucic, a close associate of Serbia's president Slobodan Milosevic.

Beogradska Banka system said it will set up a new Beogradska Banka-Group (BB-Group) for international credit and payment operations, to handle most international claims and liabilities of Yugoslav banks and companies.
Beogradska Banka groups 20 out of 100 Yugoslav banks and services almost two-thirds of the entire Serbian economy.
It will also establish its own agency to take over its members' debt and help them regain financial vitality.

An analyst with a state bank said there was an idea to create three state banking systems, two of which will be responsible for international credit and payment operations and the third one for financing agriculture.

"Beogradska Banka will resume responsibility in talks with London club creditors, Jugobanka should be in charge of dealing with succession issues with former Yugoslav republics, while Vojvodjanska is planned to finance agriculture," the source who asked not to be named told Reuters.
"Banks members of those three groups will not be able to enter any credit arrangements with foreigners on their own," the source said.
Other small and medium size banks will be left to find their place mostly in domestic banking services.
But economists said centralising the financial sector was not sustainable.

"It depends on a bank itself whether it is successful and manages to do business with the world. Its success should not depend on the government," said Slobodan Milosavljevic of the Institute for Market Research.
Another economist cautioned that centralisation can cost the economy a lot, but saw the move as a government's attempt to take control over scarce financial resources.
"Our financial situation is very bad. And one tends to seek control over something that is scarce and unlikely to become available for quite some time," the economist said.
Another analyst said: "The government only wants to establish firm control over money flows ahead of privatisation. They want to create cheap access to whatever is lucrative in this economy."
But an economist close to the government said no final decisions have been made yet.

"There are some ideas to concentrate the banking sector, but it will not involve all banks. The most acceptable idea is to merge small illiquid banks with bigger ones," the source said, speaking under condition of anonymity.
The source was hoping that the centralisation would not happen after all. "It would not lead Yugoslavia towards a liberal economy. Instead, we must seek ways to attract foreign banks over here."

Meanwhile, government officials have promised a comprehensive bank reform programme, which should begin with a clean-up of banks' balances of frozen hard currency savings and external debt, spent a long time ago.
"We want to clean up banks' balances and prepare them for market competition. Their key aim must be profit," new Yugoslav Finance Minister Bozidar Gazivoda told Reuters.
But the government was not ready to implement a wide-ranging reconstruction of the banking sector and liquidate big insolvent banks,fearing numerous company closures.
"If we decide to liquidate big banks, the entire economy will suffer," Gazivoda said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
